analysis.one_liner: Creates a USDA office to investigate and prosecute meatpackers for anticompetitive practices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and died there at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an Office of the Special Investigator for Competition Matters inside USDA's Packers and Stockyards Division. The office could subpoena records, investigate and prosecute meatpackers that violate the 1921 Packers and Stockyards Act, and bring civil cases against them directly rather than waiting on the Justice Department. It would also serve as a link between USDA and the Justice Department, FTC, and Homeland Security on competition and food supply security.
analysis.who_benefits: Livestock producers — cattle ranchers and hog farmers — who sell into markets dominated by a handful of large meatpacking companies and have limited power to challenge unfair pricing or retaliation. Consumers could benefit if more competition lowers meat prices.

how_it_helps.text: Gives USDA its own prosecutors: the Special Investigator could use subpoenas and bring civil or administrative actions against packers under the Packers and Stockyards Act without relying on DOJ.
Sets up liaison roles with DOJ and FTC on food-sector competition and with DHS on food supply security, aiming to coordinate enforcement against concentrated meatpacking firms.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies, which would face an investigator dedicated to enforcing competition rules against them, plus USDA, which would fund and staff the new office.

drawbacks.text: A new enforcement office adds federal spending and staffing, and the bill text does not specify its budget or size.

Meatpackers would face a dedicated enforcement office, and packers and industry groups argued existing antitrust laws and agencies were already sufficient and that beef prices reflected market conditions rather than concentration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main cost is the budget for a new USDA office, while the benefit is dedicated enforcement capacity in a market where four firms process the large majority of cattle. The design gives USDA authority it already nominally had under the 1921 Act but lacked dedicated staff and subpoena-driven prosecution to use, so the value depends entirely on funding and whether the administration uses it.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read it twice and sent it to the Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Tester, Grassley, and Rounds introduced the bill on June 10, 2021, with 12 cosponsors split evenly between six Republicans and six Democrats.
The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee and received no further action before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking companies avoided a dedicated USDA prosecutor focused on their conduct. Rural livestock producers kept paying into a market with no added enforcement of competition rules.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly split: the bill had 6 Republican and 6 Democratic cosponsors plus the sponsor, but no vote ever occurred.

industries.note: The four major beef packers would face a dedicated USDA office with subpoena power to investigate and sue them over anticompetitive conduct, so the bill's whole point was enforcement against them. Stopping it preserved the status quo in livestock markets.
Producers selling into concentrated markets would gain an enforcement avenue against unfair pricing and retaliation by packers.
